name: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young Type 5 (HNF1B-MODY)

clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous mutations or, very commonly, whole-gene deletions of HNF1B; a large proportion of cases arise de novo, so absence of a family history does not exclude it.
It is a multisystem disorder rather than isolated diabetes, classically the renal cysts and diabetes (RCAD) syndrome, with kidney disease often preceding or dominating the picture.
Renal features include renal cysts, renal hypoplasia or dysplasia, and progressive non-diabetic chronic kidney disease that can appear from fetal life onward.
Pancreatic involvement extends beyond beta-cell failure to hypoplasia of the pancreatic body and tail, causing exocrine insufficiency with low faecal elastase.
Unlike HNF1A and HNF4A MODY, patients are usually NOT sulfonylurea-sensitive and typically require insulin relatively early.
Associated features include genital tract malformations (for example uterine anomalies), hypomagnesaemia from renal magnesium wasting, hyperuricaemia with early gout, and deranged liver enzymes.
Consider HNF1B testing and dosage analysis in any young patient with diabetes plus unexplained renal cysts, renal dysplasia or a low serum magnesium.
The 17q12 microdeletion encompassing HNF1B may additionally be associated with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric features.
reference.pathophysiology: MODY5 is caused by heterozygous inactivating point mutations or, frequently, by heterozygous deletion of the entire HNF1B gene at chromosome 17q12; a high proportion of cases occur de novo. HNF1B encodes hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-beta, a transcription factor critical for the embryonic development and function of the kidney, pancreas, liver, biliary tract and genital tract, which explains the multisystem phenotype. In the developing kidney, HNF1B governs nephrogenesis and tubular differentiation, so haploinsufficiency produces structural anomalies such as cysts, hypoplasia and dysplasia together with tubular dysfunction including renal magnesium wasting and impaired urate handling. In the pancreas it directs both endocrine and exocrine development; its loss causes pancreatic hypoplasia with reduced beta-cell mass and progressive insulin secretory failure alongside exocrine insufficiency. Because the defect reflects reduced beta-cell mass and impaired development rather than a reversible functional channel defect, residual insulin secretion is limited and the pronounced sulfonylurea sensitivity typical of HNF1A and HNF4A MODY is generally absent, so patients tend to need insulin. Additional expression in liver and genital tract accounts for hepatic enzyme derangement and Müllerian or other genital malformations.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and other inherited cystic kidney diseases
HNF1A-MODY and HNF4A-MODY, which lack the renal structural and electrolyte features and are sulfonylurea-sensitive
Type 1 diabetes mellitus with coincidental renal disease
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic nephropathy (here nephropathy is non-diabetic and often precedes diabetes)
Other syndromic causes of renal dysplasia with diabetes
Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract from other genetic causes
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of HNF1B including dosage/deletion analysis (for example MLPA) to detect whole-gene deletions
Renal imaging (ultrasound or MRI) for cysts, hypoplasia or dysplasia
Serum magnesium and fractional excretion of magnesium for renal wasting
Serum urate and renal function with estimated GFR to stage kidney disease
Faecal elastase and liver enzymes to assess exocrine pancreatic and hepatic involvement
Pelvic imaging for uterine and genital tract anomalies where relevant
Pancreatic autoantibodies and C-peptide to exclude autoimmune diabetes
redFlags: Progressive chronic kidney disease advancing toward established renal failure and need for renal replacement
Antenatally detected hyperechogenic or cystic dysplastic kidneys, prompting evaluation for HNF1B
Symptomatic hypomagnesaemia or early-onset gout from renal tubular dysfunction
Diabetes that fails to respond to oral agents and requires early insulin
Neurodevelopmental or psychiatric features in patients with the 17q12 microdeletion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the renal phenotype, which can progress to chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure independently of glycaemic control; diabetes usually requires insulin, and the multisystem nature necessitates lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up. Outcomes vary widely depending on the severity of renal and pancreatic involvement.
pitfalls: Relying on sequencing alone and missing the common whole-gene deletion, which requires dosage analysis to detect
Excluding the diagnosis because there is no family history, when many cases are de novo
Expecting a sulfonylurea response as in HNF1A/HNF4A MODY and delaying necessary insulin
Attributing the renal disease to diabetic nephropathy when it is a primary developmental kidney disorder often predating diabetes
Overlooking hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia, genital tract anomalies or exocrine insufficiency that point to the multisystem syndrome
